etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bache, bæcche (“bank, sandbank”), from Old English beċe (“beck, brook, stream”), from Proto-West Germanic *baki, from Proto-Germanic *bakiz (“brook”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“flowing water”).

Cognate with Dutch beek (“brook, stream”), German Bach (“brook, stream”), Swedish bäck (“stream, brook, creek”). More at batch, beck.

definitions.definition: The shore of a body of water, especially when sandy or pebbly.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path […]. It twisted and turned, […] and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn. And, back of the lawn, was a big, old-fashioned house, with piazzas stretching in front of it, and all blazing with lights. 'Twas the house I'd seen the roof of from the beach.

definitions.definition: A horizontal strip of land, usually sandy, adjoining water.

quote.text: Up and down, the beach lay empty for miles.

definitions.definition: (UK dialectal, Sussex, Kent) The loose pebbles of the seashore, especially worn by waves; shingle.
(motor racing, euphemistic) Synonym of gravel trap
(sports) A dry, dusty pitch or situation, as though playing on sand.

quote.citation: 2008, Phil Shaw, The Book of Football Quotations, page 415:
quote.text: I never realised Lincoln was a seaside town. BRIAN LAWS Scunthorpe manager, after losing on a liberally sanded beach of a pitch

quote.citation: 2012, Tim Quelch, Bent Arms & Dodgy Wickets:
quote.text: The series was brought to an ironic conclusion when England became hoist by their own petard, as they lost the deciding final Test on a 'beach' of a wicket. Neither side batted well.

definitions.definition: Euphemistic form of bitch (taboo swear word).
(intransitive) To run aground on a beach.

quote.citation: 1941, Emily Carr, “Salt Water”, in Klee Wyck:
quote.text: When we finally beached, the land was scarcely less wet than the sea.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To run (something) aground on a beach.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, “Chapter 90”, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC:
quote.text: It seems that some honest mariners of Dover, or Sandwich, or some one of the Cinque Ports, had after a hard chase succeeded in killing and beaching a fine whale which they had originally descried afar off from the shore.

quote.citation: 1974, Homer, translated by Robert Fitzgerald, Iliad, Doubleday, Book Two, lines 530-31, p. 53:
quote.text: Great Aías led twelve ships from Sálamisand beached them where Athenians formed for battle.

definitions.definition: (of a vehicle) To run into an obstacle or rough or soft ground, so that the floor of the vehicle rests on the ground and the wheels cannot gain traction.
